title: Your rule, signed
hookLine: three men vow to out-pray the Prophet; his answer: i also sleep
tomorrow: how could a whole life look like one trip to Mecca?

cards: A list becomes a promise when you put your name to it, and fresh-start lists tend to arrive huge: run every morning, read every night, never touch sugar again. Three men in Medina once made plans like that.
They came to the homes of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and asked how he worshipped, and when they heard, it seemed small to them. So they raised the bar. One said: I'll pray all night, every night.
One said: I'll fast every day and never break it. One said: I'll never marry. Big promises, made with good hearts.
Then the Prophet heard what they'd said.

teach.b: His answer is in Sahih al-Bukhari. I fast, and I break my fast. I pray, and I sleep.
And I marry. Whoever turns away from my way is not of me. He doesn't mock their love.
He corrects its size. A rule nobody can keep isn't a rule; it's a mood.
Another report in Bukhari gives the measure: the deeds most beloved to Allah are the ones done steadily, even if they're small.
That's what this stretch of the path has been building, piece by piece: your prayers, your dhikr, your portion of reading, your giving, your fasts, your study, your service, your goal.
Today they go on one page, and the page gets your name. That isn't a formal vow, a nadhr, which has its own rules in Islamic law.
It's closer to what the Qur'an tells the Prophet about any decision, in Pickthall's words: "And when thou art resolved, then put thy trust in Allah."
You do the deciding; you don't carry the outcome alone. Here's the line worth repeating tonight: when people tried to out-pray the Prophet, his answer included, I also sleep.

how: Muslims often speak of keeping a small daily routine (a wird) of prayer, Qur'an and dhikr, and teachers point to the hadith that the deeds Allah loves most are the steady ones, even if small.

o: practices you chose to keep, written down and signed
the rules of prayer laid down for every Muslim
a strict set of laws a mosque gives each member

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: vowed to pray, fast and abstain nonstop
i fast and break it, pray and sleep
when resolved, put thy trust in Allah
a formal vow, with its own rules

s: the more you promise God, the more devout the plan
the Prophet corrected the three men's vows: I fast and break my fast, pray and sleep.
a hadith says the deeds Allah loves most are steady ones, even if small
reported in Sahih al-Bukhari: steady, even if small.
writing down your own rule is the same as a formal vow in Islamic law
a nadhr is a formal vow with its own rules; a written rule is resolve, then trust.

games.q: your cousin starts Ramadan prep in the fall: she plans to read the whole Qur'an every week and pray all night. by week two she's exhausted and ready to quit everything. what does the story point to?
o: shrink the plan to something she can keep, and keep it.
push through; the struggle is what makes it count.
drop the plan and wait until she feels ready again.
games.why: the Prophet answered the big vows with 'I pray, and I sleep.' steady, even if small, is the measure in the hadith.

practice: If there's paper near you, write your rule by hand in a few short lines: what you'll pray, what you'll read, what you'll give, the trait you're working on. Keep each line small enough to do on your worst week.
Read it once, slowly, and put your name under it.

wordCard.voice: Your rule: the few practices you've chosen to keep, written down, small and steady, and signed with resolve and trust.

orig.note: Arabic: resolve, a firm decision; the Qur'an's 'when thou art resolved' (3:159) uses this root.

carryVoice: Hold onto one word: committed, meaning signed, small, and still standing next month. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 5063: three men ask about the Prophet's worship and vow to pray all night, fast without break and never marry; he answers that he fasts and breaks his fast, prays and sleeps, and marries
Sahih al-Bukhari 6464 (also Sahih Muslim 783): the deeds most beloved to Allah are those done regularly, even if few

sources.q: And when thou art resolved, then put thy trust in Allah.
